narrative.text: The list of contributors to the manual, giving each author's name and institutional affiliation.

Acknowledges the WHO units that produced the training manual and the staff who led it, noting it grew out of a 2009 WHO technical consultation on research ethics in epidemic response. It thanks chapter authors, publishers who allowed material to be reused, and many external reviewers. It also credits student workshops and 2015 pilot sessions in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone that tested draft modules.

Introduces the manual's aim of providing training material on ethics in research, surveillance and patient care during epidemics, emergencies and disasters. It recalls the 2009 WHO consultation's positions on upholding ethics guidelines, the blurred line between practice and research, and adapting ethics oversight. It also explains how emergencies and disasters are understood, including natural and human-induced hazards, and ends with references.

Sets out a 90-minute overview session on ethics in epidemics, emergencies and disasters, with a plenary presentation, open discussion and group work. Facilitators are told how to shorten the session and how to run the group activity. The two case studies on allocating intravenous fluids and designing a clinical trial during a haemorrhagic fever outbreak are reproduced with their discussion questions.
A near-empty section heading for the research and surveillance part, containing only a single word.

Introduces core competence 1, on analysing the boundary between public health practice, including surveillance, and research during emergencies. It explains that this distinction still largely decides whether ethics oversight is required and lists the four learning objectives.

Sets out a 60-minute session on distinguishing public health surveillance from research, with team work on scenarios. The background defines public health and describes surveillance as a core activity that tracks disease patterns and guides control measures. It discusses why the line between research and surveillance is hard to draw, including tensions between informed consent and the goals of surveillance. The section closes with references and further reading.

Describes a session on which activities count as research during emergency response and normally need ethics review, using a team exercise where groups design a project and others judge its type. The background explains that research is usually subject to independent ethics review while public health practice often is not. It outlines categories of research, such as clinical, health services and population-based studies, with examples, followed by references.

Describes a 90-minute session on the ethical principles and requirements in current normative instruments for research and surveillance in emergencies. Participants read papers on what makes clinical research ethical, including in developing countries, before a presentation on major research ethics guidelines. The background traces the history of research ethics and the protections it offers participants, while noting debate about whether differences between research and public health practice should decide ethics review. References at the end include material on a disputed drug trial in Nigeria.

A training module, part of a course on ethics in emergencies and epidemics, on the shortcomings of existing research ethics guidelines and regulations when applied to emergencies. It gives a 120-minute session plan in which trainees test a guideline against a case study involving issues such as child vulnerability, consent across language barriers, confidentiality and conflicts of interest, then draft their own ethical framework. The background notes that most guidelines were written for clinical research in stable, well-resourced settings, while urgency in emergencies should not excuse ignoring core principles, citing the WHO panel on unregistered Ebola interventions. It then discusses altered perceptions of ethical issues, the patient–provider relationship, study integrity and ethics review, ending with references.

Introduces the second core competence of the course, on defining sound ethics review processes for public health interventions, surveillance and research in emergencies, and lists its three learning objectives on standard review, review of surveillance and variations for emergencies.

A training module describing the standard procedures that should govern ethics review of research, including public health research. Its 90-minute session plan uses a debate and a case that falls between research and surveillance to ask whether review standards could ever be altered and whether committee review is worth its cost. The background explains why prospective independent review is now broadly accepted, how multidisciplinary committees with lay members work and that review is not meant to obstruct research. It lists eleven areas a review should cover, from social value and informed consent to community participation, risk minimization and international collaboration, and ends with references and further reading.

A training module on when public health surveillance should undergo formal ethics review. Its 75-minute session plan uses a hospital testing case and group debate on which kinds of surveillance need review and which do not. The background explores the elusive line between surveillance and research, noting that research usually involves an intervention with quantifiable risk while much surveillance relies on data people may not know are collected. It discusses the ethical basis for oversight, including mutual responsibility, public trust and past misuse of HIV data, and ends by noting calls for risk-based rather than definition-based approaches, followed by references.

A training module on possible variations to standard ethics review procedures for research carried out during emergencies. Its 75-minute session plan combines group reflection, slides and two case studies asking whether projects are research or surveillance and whether expedited review or lighter consent procedures are acceptable. The background argues that research in emergencies is needed but must not exploit resource-poor settings, and sets out the debate over whether disaster survivors are inherently vulnerable. Proposed variations include expedited review, proportionality of risks and benefits, special scrutiny, generic anticipatory protocols and proactive review, with references at the end.

Introduces the third core competence of the course, on recognizing conflicts between the common good and individual autonomy in emergency surveillance. It outlines five learning objectives covering harms and benefits, when informed consent is needed, privacy and confidentiality, protection of biological materials, and when the common good may override autonomy.

A training module on the harms and benefits that public health practice and surveillance can bring to individuals and communities. Its 105-minute session plan includes writing exercises on when quarantine is justified, use of the Nuffield intervention ladder after an earthquake, a reading on the 1976 swine flu vaccine and a case about a surveillance survey that could fuel stigma. The background explains that, unlike in clinical care, benefits may go to the community while harms fall on individuals, illustrated by quarantine and mandatory vaccination. It stresses ethical practice as a way to build trust, as shown during the 2014 Ebola outbreak, and closes with references.

A training module on the factors that determine when public health surveillance requires explicit informed consent from individuals or communities. Its 60-minute session plan uses a case of a blood survey for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, with facilitator notes on whether it is research or surveillance, risks of identification and stigma, what information to disclose and whether patients may refuse. The background defines informed consent, notes its place in the Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines, and sets out the arguments for it. It then considers when consent may be waived or modified, ending with references.

A training module on protecting privacy and confidentiality during emergencies. Its 90-minute session plan centres on a case in which a village leader asks a survey team for collected data, with suggested protective steps such as engaging leaders beforehand, avoiding identifiable data and transporting questionnaires in locked boxes. The background defines privacy and confidentiality and explains why emergencies threaten them, through less controlled settings, wider data sharing, improvised recording and limited resources for secure storage. It justifies the duty of confidentiality through beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy and trustworthiness, and ends with references.

A training module on measures needed to protect data and biological materials collected during public health surveillance. Its 60-minute session plan uses a household blood-sampling case, with facilitator notes on what participants should be told, the risk of identifying positive individuals in small communities, safeguards such as broad geographical coding and restricted access, and whether results should be returned. The background describes ethical issues raised by specimens, including perceived intrusiveness, stigma that can extend to whole communities, and exploitation when products derived from samples are unaffordable locally, citing Indonesia's 2007 decision to stop sharing avian flu samples. References on stored biological materials close the section.

A training module on circumstances in which the common good may override individual autonomy in public health surveillance. It sets out a 60-minute team-based case discussion and explains that measures such as surveillance, notification, mandatory testing or treatment and quarantine each infringe rights such as privacy, consent and freedom of movement. The background explains why autonomy matters ethically and discusses when such infringements can be justified, ending with references including Mill's On liberty.

Introduces the fourth core competence of the course, on conflicts between the common good and individual autonomy in research and clinical trials during emergencies. It outlines four learning objectives on harms and benefits of research, moral theories and frameworks, waivers of consent in critical care, and improving consent in traditional communities and low-resource settings.

A training module on the potential harms and benefits to individuals and communities of conducting research during emergencies. Its 60-minute session plan has groups list harms and benefits, optionally view videos on the 1918 influenza pandemic, and discuss conflicting ethical principles and quotations on population health versus individual rights. The background notes that emergency research has sometimes caused disability and death, and raises questions about compromising scientific standards, who bears the risks of unapproved treatments and who gets first access to scarce new treatments. It stresses fair distribution of research benefits and burdens and barriers to valid consent in traditional or low-resource settings, ending with references including reports on drug trials in Nigeria.

Provides a 60-minute seminar plan for learning objective 4.2 on moral theories, in which the facilitator presents major ethical frameworks and leads discussion of their fit for research in emergencies. The background explains how utilitarianism, egalitarianism, libertarianism and rights-based theories each stress different values, and argues for a pluralistic approach. It then outlines a set of principles to weigh, each to be discussed in terms of justification, legitimacy and practicality, and closes with references including the Siracusa principles.

Sets out a 75-minute session for learning objective 4.3 on when a waiver of informed consent may be acceptable for research in critical care and emergencies, using small-group debate for and against research without consent. The facilitator then outlines current norms for consent waivers and revisits the Trovan and SARS case studies, asking whether minimal-risk conditions were met. Notes for facilitators discuss proxy consent by stressed parents, and the section ends with references on research with critically ill patients.

Presents a 90-minute session for learning objective 4.4 on improving informed consent in emergency research, especially in traditional communities and low-resource settings. Participants read the Trovan case study and related news items, then split into groups to examine questions such as the ethical challenges of such settings and how the sponsor could have avoided wrongdoing. Facilitator notes cover language and cultural barriers, community permission, and the heightened vulnerability and risk of exploitation of participants during emergencies. The section includes background material and closes with references, including studies on consent comprehension in Ghana and clinical trial ethics in Nigeria.

Introduces core competence 5, on how publication ethics relate to surveillance and research in emergencies, and lists its three learning objectives. These cover publishing data gathered during surveillance or routine care, publication bias, and ethical duties around ownership of scientific data.

Outlines a 75-minute session for learning objective 5.1 on when data from surveillance or routine clinical care may be published as scientific knowledge, built around a role play in which the facilitator seeks post-hoc ethics clearance for a paper by Balasegaram et al. Groups decide whether to grant clearance, weighing the lack of patient information and prior ethics review against social benefit. Background text stresses the strong obligation to share emergency findings quickly, and the section ends with references.

Gives a 90-minute session plan for learning objective 5.2 on publication bias and its effect on emergency response, combining readings by Godlee and Loder and by Cohen, a news video about the antiviral Tamiflu, and a case study. Small groups discuss whether the case shows publication bias, how it could be prevented or mitigated, and how it could affect emergency response. Background material explains that emergency preparedness relies on research evidence and describes proposed methods for addressing publication bias. References at the end include WHO documents on H5N1 influenza and the Model List of Essential Medicines.

Presents a 120-minute session for learning objective 5.3 on the ethical obligations of researchers, public health practitioners and publishers regarding ownership of scientific data. After readings and a video about Tamiflu, two groups debate stricter data control versus open data sharing during an emergency, to inform thinking about data-sharing policy. Participants then examine a case study on access to data on oseltamivir effectiveness, weighing data ownership against public benefit. The section closes with references and further reading on drug safety and effectiveness.

Introduces core competence 6, on ethical criteria for triage, resource allocation and standards of care in emergency response, illustrated by a photo from the 2010 Haiti earthquake. It lists four learning objectives covering triage and rationing frameworks, altered standards of care, benefit-sharing with communities under surveillance, and equitable access to unproven treatments.

Sets out a 90-minute session for learning objective 6.1 on ethical frameworks and criteria for triage and rationing in emergencies. Small groups consider questions such as which resources may need allocating, who should make triage decisions, which criteria should never be used, and whether to maximize lives or life-years saved. Further large-group discussion and a reading follow, with background on triage criteria and conflicts between the common good and individual patients. The section ends with references, including WHO discussion papers on ethics in pandemic influenza planning.

Provides a 90-minute session for learning objective 6.2 on how standards of care and treatment may be altered during emergencies, distinguishing this from triage. The first case study uses an article and video about Dr Anna Pou's actions in a hospital after a hurricane to explore moral versus legal responsibility. A second exercise uses scenarios from Levin et al. for individual reflection and group discussion, and the section closes with references.

Outlines a 105-minute session for learning objective 6.3 on benefit-sharing with communities under public health surveillance, starting with the UNESCO Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights and the line between benefits and undue inducement. Participants read Simm (2007) and discuss in groups how benefit-sharing applies to surveillance, followed by a case presentation and discussion. Background covers the history of the benefit-sharing concept. References include the Nagoya Protocol, WHO's Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Sets out a 60-minute session with reading and a debate for learning objective 6.4 on equitable access to unproven treatments during emergency research. The case study concerns post-exposure prophylaxis during an Ebola outbreak in central Africa and the tension between generating robust trial data and compassionate use to save lives now. Facilitator notes refer to the 2014 west African Ebola epidemic and a WHO panel convened that August on the ethics of investigational interventions. The section ends with references on trial designs and the ethics of experimental Ebola treatments.

Introduces core competence 7, on the professional duties of health care workers during surveillance or research in emergencies, with a photo of a clinic in Kandahar. It notes conflicts such as the duty to care, therapeutic misconception and conflicts of interest, and lists three learning objectives.

Presents a training session plan for learning objective 7.1, which asks trainees to compare the aims, values and principles of medical care ethics, public health ethics and research ethics. The 100-minute session moves from an introduction through small-group work with a comparison template, a video on disaster ethics, a case study, a role-play and a closing summary. Facilitator notes supply discussion questions on whether clinical values can be carried into public health interventions and research in emergencies. The section ends with a list of readings and references on clinical, public health and disaster ethics.

Sets out a 75-minute training session on the concept of therapeutic misconception and how it bears on the duties of health care workers who take part in research during emergencies. Facilitators introduce the idea, review three strategies for helping people tell clinical research apart from medical care, and ask participants whether these are workable given language barriers, trauma and scarce resources. A case study and role-play follow, with questions on how the misconception arises and how a physician might reduce it. The section closes with references, including qualitative studies of research participation and work on empirical bioethics.

Provides a 90-minute, highly interactive session plan on conflicts of interest faced by health care workers who join research activities during emergencies. The facilitator presents definitions, then problem-solving tools for identifying, evaluating and managing such conflicts, and a model for handling them ethically. A multi-part case study is revealed in stages, with a discussion guide steering the group through three phases of analysis. The section ends with references on research integrity and responsible conduct of research.

A glossary that defines common concepts, principles and values used in health ethics, noting that the definitions are aids to understanding rather than definitive. Entries include terms such as accountability for reasonableness, autonomy and beneficence, each with supporting citations. It opens with a photo caption about WHO support to a hospital medical records office in Sri Lanka and ends with a numbered reference list.

Lists every module of the emergency ethics course, from the overview through the core competences and their learning objectives, with the time allotted to each. It introduces the sample course timetables that follow.

Gives a sample two-day timetable for a practice-oriented version of the course, assigning learning objectives to timed sessions with breaks. Day 1 covers topics such as surveillance versus research, the three ethics frameworks, and triage and altered standards of care, while day 2 turns to ethics review, consent and use of surveillance data.

Gives a sample two-day timetable for a research-oriented version of the course, setting out which learning objectives are covered in each timed session. Sessions address topics such as what counts as research in emergencies, harms and benefits of research, conflicts of interest, therapeutic misconception and ownership of scientific data.

Annex II collects the case studies used throughout the course on ethics in epidemics, emergencies and disasters, grouped by core competence and cross-referenced to the sessions that use them. The first case asks groups how to allocate scarce intravenous fluid sets during an outbreak of viral haemorrhagic fever with limited diagnostic capacity. Later cases cover topics drawn from the course objectives, each followed by discussion questions on how problems might have been handled differently. The annex ends with contact details for WHO's Global Health Ethics Unit.

The front matter of the English training manual on ethics in epidemics, emergencies and disasters, with title pages, cataloguing data and ISBN, WHO copyright and disclaimer text, and the table of contents.
